channel_title: AI News & Strategy Daily | Nate B Jones
title: If OpenAI And Anthropic Are Discouraging You, You're Probably A Level 1 Builder.
executive_summary: Nate B Jones, in "If OpenAI And Anthropic Are Discouraging You, You're Probably A Level 1 Builder," outlines 5 distinct levels of AI building, from basic consumers to foundational researchers, to help individuals define and advance their careers. He warns that simply relying on off-the-shelf tools or basic API calls (Levels 1 and 2) is becoming a commoditized skill, with implementation costs for such integrations "going to zero by the end of the year." Jones emphasizes that true value lies in higher levels, where AI systems like SentinelAI 1.0 can even surpass human experts, demonstrated by its discovery of 27 zero-day vulnerabilities in a major enterprise ERP system.
bullets: **Level 1 Builders** are essentially consumers of AI, using off-the-shelf tools like ChatGPT or Midjourney without custom integration. Nate B Jones defines this as "If you're just using off-the-shelf tools, you're a Level 1," implying these individuals aren't really "building" in a competitive sense. Think of it like someone who only uses pre-packaged cake mixes; they can make a cake, but they aren't truly bakers creating from scratch.

**Level 2 Builders** integrate existing AI APIs, like those from OpenAI or Anthropic, into simple applications. Nate B Jones warns that the "implementation costs" for these basic API calls "are going to zero by the end of the year," making this level increasingly commoditized and non-defensible. This is like assembling IKEA furniture with a detailed instruction manual and pre-drilled holes; it requires some effort, but the core design and components are all provided.

**Level 3 Builders** dive deeper, focusing on complex prompt engineering, fine-tuning existing models, building sophisticated Retrieval Augmented Generation (RAG) systems, and crafting custom tool-using agents, often using frameworks like LangChain. Nate emphasizes that achieving robust systems at this level can "often take 4-5 months" of dedicated work. This is like a master chef who modifies classic recipes, understands the nuances of ingredients, and even combines different cooking techniques to create a unique dish.

**Level 4 Builders** adapt and modify open-source models, experiment with novel architectures, and engage in advanced AI security work, going beyond just using proprietary APIs. The speaker highlights how a new "AI-powered security scanner, SentinelAI 1.0," recently "found 27 zero-day vulnerabilities in a major enterprise ERP system that human teams missed." This is akin to an automotive engineer designing and optimizing a new engine block, rather than just driving a car or replacing standard parts.

**Level 5 Builders** are at the forefront of AI research, developing new foundational models, inventing novel training paradigms, and contributing fundamental science to the field. This level involves pushing the very boundaries of what AI can do, rather than simply applying existing technologies. Think of it like a theoretical physicist discovering new laws of nature, expanding the basic principles everyone else builds upon.

The speaker cautions that the traditional human-centric view of software security, where "A good human engineer wrote this," is becoming "a much weaker security claim" in the age of advanced AI. This shift is due to AI's ability to uncover subtle flaws and vulnerabilities that even expert human developers overlook. It is like trusting a handwritten ledger over a meticulously audited digital database; the old method, while once sufficient, is now prone to errors compared to new tools.

A major pitfall for builders at lower levels is an imbalanced focus on evaluation, with Nate B Jones stating, "Most teams today have their evaluation tests split backwards: 80% on functionality, 20% on code hygiene (naming, structure, function length)." He argues this ratio needs to be flipped or at least made "at least 50/50" for sustainable, high-quality AI systems. This is like building a house with a beautiful facade but a shaky foundation and exposed wiring; it looks good initially, but it's not truly robust or maintainable.

The "discouragement" many feel from OpenAI and Anthropic stems from their success in commoditizing basic AI capabilities, making Level 1 and 2 work feel trivial. Nate B Jones suggests that if these major players make your current work seem easy or redundant, it's a clear sign you need to level up your skills beyond simple API consumption. It's like feeling disheartened as a blacksmith when a massive factory starts mass-producing cheap, high-quality tools; your traditional craft suddenly seems less essential.

Moving beyond simple API calls and integrating existing models is critical for defensible AI building. Nate B Jones implies that merely calling APIs will not lead to a sustainable career, as the value moves up the stack to those who can customize, fine-tune, and build complex systems. This is like wanting to be an architect but only knowing how to install pre-made doors and windows; to truly build, you need to understand the structural engineering and design principles.

The economic argument presented by Nate B Jones highlights that the "implementation costs" for basic AI integrations are "rapidly approaching zero." This means the barrier to entry for simple AI applications is disappearing, making it harder for individuals or small teams to create unique value by just connecting services. It's like the price of basic raw materials plummeting, meaning you need to do something far more complex and creative with them to make a profit.

The speaker implicitly encourages builders to aspire to Level 3 and Level 4 work, where custom value creation and deep technical understanding become paramount. This involves developing a nuanced understanding of AI models beyond their surface-level functionality. This is like a mechanic who doesn't just change oil but deeply understands engine diagnostics and can rebuild complex transmissions.

The specific example of "SentinelAI 1.0" finding "27 zero-day vulnerabilities" underscores AI's growing capability in areas traditionally dominated by highly skilled human experts. This demonstrates that even in critical fields like cybersecurity, AI is not just assisting but actively surpassing human performance in certain tasks. It's like a new robotic surgeon performing intricate operations with greater precision and fewer errors than even the most experienced human doctors.

Nate B Jones's framework implicitly advises builders to choose projects that challenge them to move up the levels, rather than sticking to what is easy or already commoditized. The goal is to build expertise in areas where unique value can still be created and where large AI companies are not directly making your efforts redundant. This is like a video game where you need to master harder challenges to unlock new abilities and areas, instead of just replaying the tutorial level.
key_takeaways: Immediately stop just calling basic APIs and instead build truly custom systems. Dedicate time to learn model fine-tuning, complex prompt engineering, and RAG systems, knowing this might "take 4-5 months" to build something robust and unique. If you do not, your work will quickly become commoditized as "implementation costs are going to zero by the end of the year," leaving your skills easily replaceable.

Actively seek out opportunities to work with or adapt open-source models, or engage in AI security projects, pushing you into Level 4 building. This will allow you to create novel solutions that leverage AI's ability to find complex issues, like how "SentinelAI 1.0 found 27 zero-day vulnerabilities" in major systems. Otherwise, you'll remain stuck doing easily replaceable tasks, limited by the capabilities of pre-built proprietary tools.

Immediately re-evaluate your project's testing and evaluation strategy to prioritize code quality alongside functionality. Set a strict rule that at least 50% of your evaluation tests must check for code hygiene (naming, structure, function length), not just whether the code works. Nate B Jones warns that "most teams currently have this split backwards at 80% functionality, 20% hygiene"; without this balance, your systems will be brittle, unmaintainable, and prone to hidden flaws despite appearing functional.

technical_terms.API (Application Programming Interface): A set of rules and tools that allows different software applications to communicate with each other. Think of it like a restaurant menu that tells you what dishes you can order and how to order them, without needing to know how the kitchen works.
technical_terms.Fine-tuning: The process of taking a pre-trained AI model and further training it on a smaller, specific dataset to adapt it for a particular task or domain. Think of it like taking a general-purpose chef and training them specifically to become a master pastry chef.
technical_terms.Prompt Engineering: The art and science of crafting inputs (prompts) for large language models to elicit desired outputs. Think of it like learning to ask very specific, well-structured questions to get the exact answer you need from a knowledgeable but literal assistant.
technical_terms.Retrieval Augmented Generation (RAG): An AI architecture that combines a large language model with an external knowledge base or document retrieval system to generate more accurate and contextually relevant responses. Think of it like giving a smart student access to a comprehensive library before they write an essay, ensuring their answers are well-informed and current.
technical_terms.LangChain: An open-source framework designed to simplify the development of applications that use large language models, making it easier to chain together different components like models, data sources, and tools. Think of it like a toolkit for building complex robots, where each tool helps you connect different parts like arms, sensors, and brains.
technical_terms.Zero-day vulnerability: A software flaw that is unknown to the vendor (meaning they have "zero days" to fix it) and is actively being exploited by attackers. Think of it like a secret, hidden weak spot in a fortress that invaders discover and exploit before the builders even know it exists.
technical_terms.Open-source model: An AI model whose underlying code, architecture, and sometimes even training data are publicly available for anyone to inspect, modify, and use. Think of it like a blueprint for a machine that anyone can download, customize, and build upon.
technical_terms.Code hygiene: The practice of writing clean, readable, well-structured, and maintainable code, including aspects like clear naming conventions, consistent formatting, and appropriate function lengths. Think of it like keeping your kitchen organized and clean, so you can easily find ingredients, follow recipes, and prevent messes from escalating.
technical_terms.ERP system (Enterprise Resource Planning: A type of software system used by organizations to manage and integrate various business processes, such as finance, human resources, manufacturing, and supply chain. Think of it like the central nervous system of a large company, coordinating all its different organs and functions.
technical_terms.API consumption: The act of using an API provided by another service or application, typically by sending requests and receiving responses. Think of it like ordering food from a restaurant's menu – you're consuming the service they offer.
